result.target_summary: Professional artists and designers use NVIDIA partner products for creative and design work. Generative AI is expanding the market for workstation-class GPUs as enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications on-premises.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation: Both disclosures focus on the specific use of NVIDIA technology by professional designers and artists for creative work. D009 (2023) mentions visual effects, buildings, and products. D008 (2024) mentions visual effects, buildings, and products, and explicitly links this to workstation-class GPUs. The subject matter (professional design/creative use) is identical.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation: The 2024 disclosure (nvda_2024_1_D008) specifically describes the use of NVIDIA products by 'Professional artists, architects and designers' and the expansion of the 'workstation-class GPUs' market due to generative AI. In 2025, the closest topic is Professional Visualization (nvda_2025_1_D024), which discusses serving the 'Professional Visualization market' and 'design and manufacturing' workflows. However, the 2024 disclosure is focused on the specific end-user base (artists/designers) and the resulting market expansion for workstation GPUs, whereas the 2025 disclosure (nvda_2025_1_D024) is framed as a market segment service strategy involving ISV optimization. Furthermore, the 2025 disclosure nvda_2025_1_D006 mentions 'workstation GPU demand growing' but focuses on enterprise/enterprise software use cases rather than the specific 'professional artists and designers' user base definition found in the 2024 text. There is no exact counterpart defining the 'Professional artists and designers' user group as the primary subject of a segment or business model statement in the same way. The 2024 D008 is a unique observation of user base expansion, not a segment definition like D011/D012

comparisons.peer_topic: Hyperscale Customer Base and Product Applications
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's data center products, including server CPUs, GPU accelerators, and adaptive SOCs, are purchased by large public cloud providers and hyperscale private data centers. These customers incorporate the products into servers for web applications, public cloud services, and AI workloads such as generative AI models.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies identify enterprise on-premises generative AI workloads as a key driver for their hardware sales, though they target different segments of the AI infrastructure stack. NVIDIA describes how enterprise customers deploy AI applications on-premises, driving demand for its workstation-class GPUs, while AMD describes how hyperscale data centers use GPU accelerators to support AI workloads such as generative AI models. The primary difference is that NVIDIA highlights the specific growth in the workstation segment for on-premises development, whereas AMD focuses on the broader hyperscale public cloud and private data center server market.

sentences.text: In addition, generative AI is expanding the market for our workstation-class GPUs, as more enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises.

Hyperscale data centers use these products to operate web-based applications or to support public cloud computing and storage service offerings, including but not limited to AI workloads such as generative AI models.

comparisons.peer_summary: This solution enables organizations to use generative AI technologies while addressing privacy and compliance needs.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address the deployment of generative AI technologies within organizational environments, specifically highlighting the on-premises or private nature of these deployments. NVIDIA notes that enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises, utilizing workstation GPUs. Broadcom explicitly lists 'Private AI' as a solution that enables organizations to use generative AI technologies while addressing privacy and compliance needs. Both reflect a trend toward keeping AI workloads and data internal rather than in the public cloud.

sentences.text: In addition, generative AI is expanding the market for our workstation-class GPUs, as more enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises.
• Private AI: This solution enables organizations to use generative AI technologies while addressing privacy and compliance needs of the organization.

comparisons.peer_topic: Software strategy and open source contributions
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel aims to optimize AI frameworks and maintains the OpenVINO toolkit for deep learning inference. In 2024, Intel launched the Open Platform for Enterprise AI under the Linux Foundation and contributed oneAPI specifications to the UXL Foundation to enable open, multi-vendor programming across accelerators.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies disclose the expansion of generative AI as a business driver, though they focus on different layers of the software and hardware stack. NVIDIA identifies generative AI as expanding the market for its hardware (workstation GPUs) for on-premises deployment. Intel focuses on the software strategy, noting the launch of the Open Platform for Enterprise AI and the use of its OpenVINO toolkit to accelerate deep learning inference for generative AI use cases across various domains including cloud and edge.

sentences.text: In addition, generative AI is expanding the market for our workstation-class GPUs, as more enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises.

Our OpenVINO™ toolkit is an open source toolkit that accelerates deep learning inference on our processors across various use cases, such as generative AI, computer vision, audio, and language with industry standard models.
In 2024 we launched the Open Platform for Enterprise AI under the Linux Foundation to accelerate deployment of generative AI use cases through industry standard modular microservice architecture.

comparisons.peer_summary: CNBU data center sales were driven by server demand in cloud and enterprise markets, with growth fueled by the shift of infrastructure and workloads to the cloud and the memory-intensive nature of AI data-centric workloads.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures link generative AI to significant demand for infrastructure resources, specifically memory-intensive workloads. NVIDIA states that generative AI is expanding the market for workstation-class GPUs as enterprises develop applications on-premises. Micron explains that cloud servers supporting AI and data-centric workloads require significantly increasing quantities of DRAM, including HBM, because turning data into insight is becoming memory-centric. Both identify AI workloads as a primary growth driver for their respective component technologies (GPUs and memory).

sentences.text: In addition, generative AI is expanding the market for our workstation-class GPUs, as more enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises.

Cloud servers supporting AI and data-centric workloads require significantly increasing quantities of DRAM, including HBM, and NAND as the task of turning data into insight becomes increasingly memory-centric.

comparisons.peer_summary: Qualcomm envisions generative AI becoming ubiquitous, expanding beyond smartphones and PCs into industries such as IoT, XR, and automotive.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures discuss the expansion of generative AI into new markets and applications. NVIDIA highlights the expansion into enterprise on-premises workstation use cases. Qualcomm envisions generative AI becoming ubiquitous and expanding beyond traditional devices (smartphones/PC) into IoT, XR, and automotive. While NVIDIA focuses on the enterprise/server-to-workstation pipeline, Qualcomm focuses on the edge device expansion, but both confirm generative AI is driving broader market adoption beyond initial core segments.

sentences.text: In addition, generative AI is expanding the market for our workstation-class GPUs, as more enterprise customers develop and deploy AI applications with their data on-premises.
Building on the smartphone and PC foundation, we envision generative AI becoming ubiquitous, continuing to expand into industries and applications such as IoT, XR and automotive.
